scenario: It's close night, mid-integration. Four stations stand between the finance team and sign-off: a variance triage, the contingents desk, the trust reconciliation, and the deal desk. Work each one with the right Copilot surface, verify like a reviewer, and sign off with the code the data yields.

rooms.title: Variance Triage
rooms.narrative: The flux review flagged Specialty Distribution: one profit center's core commissions have been eroding against budget since April — softening cat-property rates, and it's getting worse every month. The controller signs off on a name, not a feeling. Find the profit center and bring its id.
labSteps: Open 'profit-center-pnl.csv' — Excel with Copilot or the Analyst agent; Analyst handles the multi-month pivot best.
Scope the question: segment = 'Specialty Distribution', account = 'Core commissions', months April through June 2026.
Ask for percent variance to budget by profit center by month — you are looking for a worsening trend, not a single bad month.
One profit center's variance deteriorates every month across the quarter while its peers hold roughly flat. That trajectory is the finding.
Verify like a reviewer: compute the three monthly variances for your candidate by hand from the raw rows and confirm each month is worse than the last.
Sign off with that profit center's id exactly as it appears in the file, hyphen included. Example format: PC-999
hints: Ask for the April, May, and June core-commission variance percentages side by side per Specialty Distribution profit center. The one you want steps down every month — a rate story, not a one-time item.
It's the coastal programs book: core commissions run five percent under budget in April, nine under in May, thirteen under in June. Sign off with its profit-center id, hyphen included.
skillsTaught: Trend questions vs outlier questions in a flux review
Scoping Analyst prompts to segment, account, and period
Re-deriving a Copilot finding from raw rows before sign-off

rooms.title: Contingents Desk
rooms.narrative: Contingent commissions are booked on accrual — and accruals rest on loss ratios. One carrier's book has been deteriorating all half, and by June its YTD loss ratio sits above the profit-share threshold in its agreement. If that holds, the accrual is at risk and the auditors will ask why it wasn't flagged. Name the carrier.
labSteps: Open 'carrier-commission-statements.csv' — Analyst or Excel Copilot both work here.
For each carrier, compare 'carrier_ytd_loss_ratio' to 'contingent_threshold_loss_ratio' month by month through June 2026.
Find the carrier whose YTD loss ratio ends June ABOVE its threshold — the trend matters: it started the year comfortably below and crossed during the half.
Corroborate with the accrual column: the same carrier's June contingent accrual has already been zeroed out. Two independent signals, one finding.
For contrast, note the best-performing book in the file — a reviewer states the range, not just the exception.
Sign off with the FIRST WORD of the carrier's name, all caps. Example format: RIDGELINE
hints: Plot or tabulate each carrier's YTD loss ratio against its own threshold across the six months. Only one line crosses its threshold and keeps climbing; every other carrier ends June below theirs.

The carrier is a coastal property and casualty specialist: its YTD loss ratio ran 0.48 in January and ends June at 0.83 against a 0.60 threshold, and its June accrual is zero. The code is the first word of its name.
skillsTaught: Reading loss-ratio trends against contingent thresholds
Corroborating a finding with a second, independent signal
Turning an Analyst readout into an audit-ready flag

rooms.title: Trust Rec
rooms.narrative: Fiduciary cash is the one account nobody gets to be approximately right about. The June premium trust ledger and the trust bank statement don't tie, and the rec rubric defines exactly what counts as an exception. Work the rec, count the exceptions, and identify the money nobody can explain.
labSteps: Open 'premium-trust-ledger.csv' and 'trust-bank-statement.csv' side by side, and keep 'close-room-rubric.md' open — its exception definition is the whole game.
Ask Excel Copilot or Analyst to match ledger rows to bank lines on the policy id embedded in each bank description, then to list everything that fails to match cleanly in either direction.

Apply the rubric's four exception types one at a time: premiums collected but never remitted, duplicate remittances, bank receipts with no policy in the ledger, and ledger remittances that never hit the bank.
Count per the rubric: each exception ROW counts once, no matter how many things are wrong with it.
One bank receipt carries no policy reference at all — money in the trust account from a payer the ledger has never heard of. Identify that payer from the bank description.
Verify the count by listing the exception rows individually before you trust the total.
Sign off with the exception count immediately followed by the unidentified payer's first word, all caps, no space. Example format: 4PELICAN
hints: Work the four rubric buckets separately, then add: several June premiums show as received but have no remittance and no matching bank debit; one remittance appears twice in the bank statement (its description says so); one credit has no policy reference; and one stale item from May sits in the ledger but never reached the bank.

The buckets come to three unremitted, one duplicate, one unidentified receipt, and one stale May item. The mystery payer is an energy company that paid by ACH with no policy reference — its first word, in caps, follows the count.
skillsTaught: Two-file reconciliation with Copilot on a defined rubric
Counting exceptions by row, not by defect

rooms.title: Deal Desk
rooms.narrative: Corp dev needs two answers on Project Lighthouse before the partner call: how concentrated is the target's carrier book, and what's wrong with the seller's proposed earn-out. Both answers are sitting in the data room — if you brief Copilot to read it like a diligence analyst.
labSteps: Open the Project Lighthouse data room folder ('data-room/' in the lab data): the target overview, 3-year financials, carrier contract summary, and the seller's earn-out term sheet.
Use Copilot Chat over the files (or a Researcher-style brief): Goal, Context, Expectations, Source — ask for a concentration read and a term-sheet risk read as two separate answers.
From 'carrier-contract-summary.md': find the top carrier's share of the target's core commissions, as a whole-number percentage.
From 'earnout-term-sheet.md': find the structural defect in the earn-out — the one word a reviewer would circle in the mechanics.
Verify both against the source text: quote the sentence in each document that states your answer. If you can't quote it, you haven't found it.
Sign off with the percentage immediately followed by the defect word, all caps, no space or percent sign. Example format: 55CLAWBACK
hints: The concentration figure is stated outright in the carrier contract summary — the top carrier is the same one the contingents desk just flagged, which is exactly why the number matters. For the term sheet, read the payout mechanics: what limit would you expect to see that isn't there?
The share is a whole number in the high thirties, and the earn-out includes contingent commissions with no ceiling on the payout — the defect word is the adjective for an earn-out missing its cap.
skillsTaught: Briefing Copilot across a multi-file data room
Extracting stated figures vs inferring them
Spotting what a term sheet omits, and quoting sources for sign-off
